A tool with no adoption and no inspection is a good intention. This file is the mechanism that makes the gym actually run: what it is for, the countable results, the inputs it moves, and how it gets inspected. Companion to learn/VALIDATION.md — same shape, one layer up. That flywheel guards whether a unit teaches; this one guards whether judgment improves.

The challenge, worked backwards

Recurring challenge: judgment does not build from reading. The corpus grows every month; the ability to make a defensible call on a live decision does not follow it.

Three countable results (the ORR pattern — AWS named fewer, shorter, smaller incidents):

Result Counted as
More reps Cases scored, not briefed
Sharper diagnosis Share of reps where you named the crux before the red team named it
Fewer soft spots Rubric dimensions scoring below 4

The controllable inputs

Input metric Definition Source Why it's controllable
Reps / week A scored memo landed in the ledger. Target: 1 Rep log You decide whether to sit down
Unprompted crux rate Did your stated crux survive the red team, without it being handed to you from the case's canon list? Red-team output Improves with reps and with reading the right thing
Dimensions below 4 Count of the six rubric dimensions under 4 on the latest rep Scores table Each one names a specific drill
Shelf debt closed Canon notes the red team flagged as would have changed this memo, that you then actually read Shelf debt table A short, evidence-ranked list
Calibration error |stated probability − outcome| on the forecast attached to each call Rep log, scored when resolvable Forces a number instead of a hedge
Sizing coherence Share of reps where the red team judged the pass / probe / commit size consistent with the stated probability Red-team output, scored immediately Calibration alone doesn't pay; the size you attach to it does. Unlike calibration, it needs no resolution date

Explicitly not inputs. 24 modules, 82 books, 352 cross-links, 55 site pages, ~1.5M words ingested. These measure corpus size. They are outputs of a production mechanism that already works well, and none of them moves judgment. The rubric in README.md lists "vanity metrics" as a below-a-masters tell — that applies to this repo's own dashboard.

The three legs

Leg What it is Lives in
Tool Six-dimension rubric, one-page memo spec, case template README.md, CASE-TEMPLATE.md
Adoption One rep a week, chosen from a menu of three sizes; the rep is scheduled, and a skipped week is logged as a row JUDGMENT-LEDGER.md
Inspection Every rep scored on the rubric; monthly read of the ledger for the pattern; the meta-question after every red team JUDGMENT-LEDGER.md

Adoption: why this failed once, and the fix

Honest record. The tool was complete on 2026-06-06. Case 01 was briefed the same day and the memo was never written. Sixteen weeks against a stated cadence of one case a week: zero scored reps.

Nothing in the loop cost anything when a week was skipped, so skipping was the dominant strategy. This is the failure the Bezos canon note already predicts — "the mechanism is only as live as the incentives underneath it." Three changes, each borrowed from mechanism design:

  1. Log the deviation; don't leave a hole. A missed week gets a row in the rep log with reason skipped. An absence you can see is a cost; an absence you can't is free.
  2. A menu, not a mandate. Every week offers three sizes — full memo (~90 min), crux-only (~25 min), single-figure call (~10 min). The small option exists so the streak survives a bad week. A 10-minute rep scores and counts; a skipped 90-minute rep does not.
  3. Reps are the allocated resource. Treat them like budget or headcount: 52 a year, spent or forfeited, tracked in one place. This is the cycle-time-as-finite-resource idea applied to a system of one.

Inspection: three altitudes

  • Per rep — the red team scores all six dimensions, names the bear case, and names the boardroom question that sinks you. No rep closes unscored.
  • Per month — read the ledger for the pattern, not the score: which dimension is consistently soft, whether the crux rate is moving, how many weeks were skipped.
  • Meta — the question below, which inspects the corpus rather than the rep.

The meta-question

After every red team, answer exactly one question:

Which canon note, had I actually read it, would have changed this memo?

The answer goes in the Shelf debt table in the ledger. This is the correction-of-error move: AWS's incident template asks "would any ORR recommendations have reduced or avoided the impact of this event?", so every failure audits the mechanism meant to prevent it. Here, every rep audits the shelf.

Three effects:

  • It produces a reading list ranked by evidence instead of by coverage.
  • It is the only honest test of whether the 82 notes earn their keep.
  • It collapses two of the repo's named structural gaps — 33 unapplied books, 14 sources-only clusters — into one queue. A book stays unapplied until a rep needs it, and then it jumps the line.

Rule: if three consecutive reps name the same note, that note is the next thing you read and the next practitioner application note you write.

Iteration

When the red team repeats the same critique across three cases, the fix belongs in the tool, not in the next rep — amend the memo spec or the rubric in README.md and log it below. Same rule as the learn/ flywheel: a repeated fix becomes a template change.
